journal_name: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association

abstracts.abstract: BACKGROUND: Current approaches to clinical decision support systems predominantly rely on rule-based mechanisms that inadequately capture the dynamic and contextual nature of clinical reasoning in real-world healthcare settings. This limitation fundamentally constrains the effectiveness of health IT interventions in improving patient outcomes. OBJECTIVE: This study proposes a novel theoretical framework—the Adaptive Clinical Cognition Model (ACCM)—that fundamentally reconceptualizes clinical decision-making as a complex adaptive system rather than a linear input-output process. METHODS: Through systematic analysis of 847 clinical decision episodes across three diverse healthcare systems, we applied complexity theory and distributed cognition principles using grounded theory methodology. The ACCM was iteratively refined through expert validation involving 23 practicing clinicians across multiple specialties. RESULTS: The framework identifies five critical dimensions of clinical cognition: temporal dynamics, contextual integration, epistemic uncertainty management, collaborative distribution, and adaptive learning. Unlike traditional models that characterize clinical decisions as static events, ACCM reveals how clinical reasoning emerges from iterative interactions among clinicians, patients, and information systems. The framework demonstrated superior explanatory power for 78% of previously anomalous clinical decision patterns that existing models failed to account for. CONCLUSIONS: The ACCM represents a paradigm shift in understanding clinical decision-making, offering direct implications for the design of next-generation decision support systems that accommodate the inherent complexity of healthcare delivery.

OBJECTIVE: To develop and validate an enhanced integrated model for evaluating health information technology adoption and implementation outcomes in healthcare organizations. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Building upon the DeLone and McLean Information System Success Model and Technology Acceptance Model, this study introduces novel contextual integration mechanisms and workflow alignment constructs specifically applicable to healthcare settings. The enhanced framework was validated through a meta-analytic review of 89 studies comprising 24,847 healthcare professionals across diverse institutional contexts globally. RESULTS: The enhanced model demonstrated substantially improved explanatory power (R² improved from 0.51 to 0.73) compared to existing frameworks. Novel constructs—particularly organizational readiness and workflow compatibility—emerged as critical success factors, explaining 31% of previously unaccounted variance in health IT adoption outcomes. The model demonstrated robust generalizability across different health IT implementations, including electronic health records and telehealth platforms. DISCUSSION: These findings suggest that existing technology adoption frameworks require substantial modification when applied to healthcare contexts. The enhanced model provides more accurate predictions of implementation success and identifies modifiable factors amenable to intervention. Practical implications include the ability to conduct pre-implementation assessments that predict adoption outcomes with greater accuracy. CONCLUSION: This enhanced evaluation framework offers improved theoretical understanding and practical guidance for health IT implementation, enabling more targeted strategies for improving adoption rates and realizing the full potential of health information systems.

OBJECTIVE: To design and implement CareNet, a novel distributed architecture enabling privacy-preserving collaborative analytics across institutional boundaries using electronic health records without compromising data sovereignty or patient privacy. MATERIALS AND METHODS: CareNet integrates federated machine learning with blockchain-based governance and homomorphic encryption to enable multi-institutional collaborative analytics while preserving data privacy. The system architecture was designed through a participatory design process involving informaticians, clinicians, and compliance officers from seven academic medical centers. Security verification was conducted through formal methods and penetration testing. RESULTS: CareNet enables participating institutions to jointly develop and validate predictive models without centralizing patient data, achieving model performance comparable to centralized training (AUC: 0.89 vs 0.91). The architecture supports cross-institutional queries with latency under 3 seconds through novel consensus mechanisms optimized for healthcare workloads. The blockchain governance layer provides immutable audit trails satisfying regulatory requirements including HIPAA compliance. CONCLUSIONS: CareNet demonstrates the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving collaborative health data analytics at scale, enabling research consortia and population health initiatives that were previously impossible due to privacy constraints. This architecture establishes a new paradigm for secure, decentralized health data infrastructure that maintains institutional autonomy while enabling collective intelligence for advancing medical knowledge and improving public health informatics.

OBJECTIVE: To develop and evaluate ClinicalBERT-Plus, an enhanced contextual language model specifically designed for clinical text understanding that substantially improves upon existing clinical natural language processing systems. MATERIALS AND METHODS: ClinicalBERT-Plus builds upon general-purpose transformer architectures through domain-specific pretraining on a curated corpus of 4.2 million clinical notes from diverse specialties. We introduce a novel entity relationship attention mechanism that explicitly models clinical concepts and their semantic relationships. The model was evaluated against existing clinical NLP systems using established benchmark datasets encompassing named entity recognition, relation extraction, and clinical concept normalization tasks. RESULTS: ClinicalBERT-Plus demonstrated significant improvements across all evaluated tasks. Entity extraction achieved 94.2% accuracy (F1: 0.92) and relation classification achieved 89.7% accuracy, representing relative improvements of 15% and 12% respectively over previous state-of-the-art models. Performance gains were particularly pronounced for rare conditions and specialized clinical terminology, with relative improvements exceeding 20%. The model exhibited robust performance across different clinical domains and institutional settings. DISCUSSION: The substantial performance improvements enable more reliable extraction of clinical information from unstructured text, supporting clinical decision support applications and large-scale health data analytics initiatives. Practical applications include automated coding assistance, clinical trial matching, and adverse event detection from clinical narratives. CONCLUSION: ClinicalBERT-Plus represents a significant advancement in clinical text mining capabilities, with the potential to accelerate clinical research and improve healthcare delivery through more accurate automated analysis of clinical documentation.
